utterances.text: Looking at Prosecution Exhibit P359, is it correct, Mr. Radic, that this is a document from the Petrovac Crisis Staff referring to the previous document, that is, the June 22nd order of the ARK Crisis Staff, and informing the ARK Crisis Staff that, pursuant to its decision, the following steps, enumerated in the document, by Petrovac have been taken?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, only under one of the items here it says that some of the people were removed at an earlier date, I think it's 1-2-3-4, where they say that they have been dismissed earlier on, which means that this was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. done pursuant not to this decision but to their own decisions. Although I have to comment on this particular document by saying something I said already before, that it does not bear Mr. Brdjanin's signature. The signature seems to be that of his secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And while you're correct that the Petrovac document indicates that some --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Not from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not referring to that part of your testimony, Mr. Radic. I'm actually referring to your comment about one of the items in the Petrovac document. You indicated that that document indicated that some Muslims were sacked before the order. I just wanted to point your attention to the sentence thereafter, which states: "The remaining employees have been sacked now, with the exception of one employee who was due to complete his tasks but will be sacked after that."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could next direct your attention to Prosecution's next in order, a 13 July 1992 document bearing the ERN P005-4023.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P360.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I misstated the ERN, which I think is correctly stated as P000-7104 through 7108, at least in the ERN original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, if I could direct your attention to the first lengthy enumerated item under the heading "The following conclusions can be drawn from the information submitted." Looking at the very last item bulleted there, which I believe will be found on the second page, which states: "The decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Banja Luka, Number 03531/92, dated 22 June 1992, on filling vacant management and other posts valid for the running of the economy, was implemented in the public security station." That's another indication of a municipal Crisis Staff response to an ARK directive; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, in the Krajina, Muslims were dismissed from the police, from postal services, from hospitals, even music teachers lost their positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this -- these dismissals were sometimes referred to as, by euphemistic titles, such as balancing or differentiation of personnel; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Particularly when we're talking about the music teachers. Because they did not have any access to any relevant information, unlike, of course, those employed at the postal offices or the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And these balancing orders, or differentiation of personnel orders, these dismissals, came from Pale, is that right, came from the very top?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know if this term of differentiation of personnel was used or not, but -- although I know -- I don't know where it originates from, that is, but I know that it was indeed applied at the municipal level, under such a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And with that clarification, is it correct that the orders for that to be applied at the municipal level came from the very top, came from Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: They did not. They did not come from the very top, but from the level immediately superior to us, to the municipality. There were maybe one or two instructions that arrived directly from the top, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, let me direct your attention again to the interview of July 2001, and specifically to page 27. And I'll begin at line 13 of page 27. That was Mr. Grady asking beginning of the questions, "Q. But the fact is that Mr. Brdjanin was a very powerful man, was he not?" And you said: "A. But not as a -- I wanted to tell you about this. I wanted to draw your attention to the fact that power did not come from the Crisis Staff which only lasted a brief period, because many of the decisions he made I simply rejected. The power of these people came from higher authorities, from their authorities as deputies, as ministers and things like that." And Ms. Korner asked you: "Q. I'm sorry. What decisions that he made did you reject?" And you said: "A. I refused to replace directors, managers who were not members of the SDS. And then I had to use the authority of Radovan Karadzic to draw his attention of what was going on here in the field. Of course that was not forgotten and he was not alone. There were others who wanted to do the same. I confronted him when he wanted to replace the dean, and so on. Also, the issue of the balancing of personnel. But that balancing of personnel did not come from his head. That came from the very top."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It was the dean -- the rector of the university and not the dean of a faculty that was in question there, and I really confronted him on that issue. What is at point here is that everyone wants to say that Brdjanin had a lot of clout. However, his decisions were not really that much adhered to, at least not by those who had their own head to think with. And that was the reason why I confronted him, drawing his attention to the fact that nobody can remove a rector that the university is an independent institution, and those who know who a rector is, what sort of a person he is, would never have done that. And that's the gist of the matter. That's why I entered into a conflict with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you wanted to point out two things to Ms. Korner in the July 2001 interview: First, that you confronted Mr. Brdjanin about the issue surrounding the possible termination or replacement of the rector; and two, that in any event, the balancing of personnel did not come from Mr. Brdjanin's head; it came "from the very top." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I find it difficult now to say whether he received it from the top or not. But I know that this term "balancing of personnel" was something that was being accepted and applied. Perhaps a good starting point for this was the fact that the same thing happened on the Croat and Bosniak sides as well. So that's why they wanted perhaps to even things out, also with the policies in Republika Srpska. Even today, after all the things that happened in Sarajevo, you have very few Serbs holding positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That may be a good starting point, Mr. Radic, and so let's continue with some of the other information you provided during the course of that interview to the Office of the Prosecutor. If I can direct your attention and the Court's attention and counsel's attention to page 43, lines 17 through 21. And this is you speaking, Mr. Radic: "The balancing instructions came from Pale, the balancing of personnel, which was then supposed to be implemented on the field. And it was a reflection of what was happening in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when it came from the higher authority here, then that's when the implementation began."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That's what I said a moment ago. It only started happening in our part of the field as soon as it happened on the other sides as well. And probably then someone said: You should start doing the same thing. Because in the post offices, in the police in Republika Srpska, there were non-Serb employees, whereas on the other side, everything was actually cleansed of Serbs: the police, the judiciary, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the course of that interview, you also pointed out two additional reasons, Mr. Radic, why you knew and concluded that the balancing instructions had come from Pale. The first was the fact that balancing was implemented all over RS, that you could not have a situation where it was just -- you didn't have a situation where it was just implemented in one place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Not only in the entire Republika Srpska. It was done in the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina. It took place first in Herceg-Bosna and in other parts of Bosnia where that was under Bosniak control, and even in Croatia, if you will, before it started happening in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, may I just interrupt you. Is it your answer that you say this was done in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the instructions of Pale? Because that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but that Pale went ahead and did that because it was something that was sent out to the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because it happened in the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, it was quite a long question and it started off with "balancing instructions coming from Pale," but then the second sentence, the question said: "Two additional reasons why you knew the balancing instructions had come from Pale." Then the first was the fact balancing was implemented. The trouble is when the question gets fairly long it's not surprising that the witness might understand it in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to see whether clarity, whether we can seek some clarification. Mr. Tieger, the witness seems to not have fully understood the question that has been clarified, I would say, and you got some comment that the question was very long, which is, as such, true. Whether it makes the question not comprehensible any more is a different matter, but the shorter the better. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With that guidance, Mr. Radic, I will try to break down the question. First of all, I indicated that I would direct your attention to portions of the interview in which you indicated two different reasons why you knew and concluded that the balancing instructions came from Pale. Let me focus on the first one. Did you indicate in July of 2001 that one of the reasons why you knew they had come from Pale was that the instructions were implemented all over Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you indicate that an additional reason why you knew that was because there was a document which was brought to the Crisis Staff in order to be implemented, a document from Pale referring to the balancing?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know, because I didn't see the document. Quite possibly, I said that a document existed; however, I never saw such a document about this balancing business.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I understood your responses in the interview correctly, and please correct me if I'm mistaken and I'll be more than happy to direct you to particular portions, I think you indicated indeed that you had not seen the document, but that someone brought the document to the Crisis Staff saying that he had such a document and it needed -- from Pale and it needed to be implemented. Is that essentially right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Somebody said that a document had been brought from Pale and that it had to be implemented. I personally did not see that document. Somebody said. And that's what I wish to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Perhaps I'm just missing it, but I'm not finding in the transcript of the evidence in the previous case the bit of Mr. Tieger's question that says, "I think you indicated indeed you had not seen the document but someone brought the document to the Crisis Staff saying that he had such a document and it needed to be implemented." This may be just be me missing the passage, but at the moment I don't have that reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if there's any doubt, please quote literally and indicate the exact source.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, is it helpful if I indicate I'm referring to the July interview and not to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I beg your pardon. That was a slip of the tongue. I realised it was that. When I said transcript, in fact I'm looking at the July interview, yes. And my question applies to that. Yes, 16th of July. One is July 01 and one is July 02. So this is 16 July 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think the witness has responded, but I will be happy to read out the portion of the transcript that prompted the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have a page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a different point, Your Honour. The witness has responded. The point is that Mr. Tieger's question purported to include a quite detailed summary, whether it was a quote or intended as a detailed pair paraphrase, and I'm asking where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could first indicate the page number, Mr. Tieger, so Mr. Stewart is in a position to find the right place where you referred to and then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 43 and 44, Your Honour. And in addition, if I could direct counsel's intention to page 22128 of the Brdjanin testimony. So I'll be happy to read both of those. Let me begin with the testimony and see if that resolves the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll see, shall we.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this begins at line 14. Question by Ms. Korner: "Q. Can I just ask you while we're on this page, what did you mean by your answer: 'It was seen by the person who brought it to the Crisis Staff to be adopted'? Do you mean the person who brought it to the Crisis Staff had seen the original instructions from Pale? "A. I assume so. "Q. Yes, but this is what you were telling us. Who was the person who told you that the instructions came from Pale? "A. I can't remember who told me about this. I know that I was told that differentiation of staff should be implemented and this should be implemented throughout Republika Srpska -- not just in Republika Srpska, but also in Sarajevo, Zagreb, et cetera. As a result it was necessary to implement this in our area too." I should finish that. "There must have been a document because I don't think someone in the Crisis Staff would have said let's differentiate the staff. I don't think he would have done this on his own initiative. And this is the euphemism I have referred to."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my question was directed to this, and my suggestion now is that in fact that passage that Mr. Tieger has read out was not accurately expressed by him in the question he put to the witness, and that Your Honour's suggestion a few minutes ago that if there is any doubt or -- I'm paraphrasing Your Honour now - risk of difficulty, that it would be safer to quote directly from the material rather than to attempt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the line that someone brought it to the Crisis Staff? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And said -- Ms. Cmeric will bring it back for me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated I was going to read two different portions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you still have to read the second portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first listen, then, to the second portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. This is page 43, beginning at line 17. "The balancing instructions came from Pale, the balancing of personnel, which was then supposed to be implemented on the field. And it was a reflection on what was happening in the other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And when it came from the higher authority here, then that's when the implementation began. "Q. How do you know that the instructions to balance, as you put it, the workers whatever came from Pale?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RADIC
utterances.text: "A. There is a document." Question by Ms. Korner: "Q. Right." "A. Which you saw. It was seen by the person who brought it to the Crisis Staff to be adopted. And then you need to know that that was not implemented only here, it was implemented in the whole of the Republika Srpska so you could not have a situation where this Crisis Staff would send this to Trebinje."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not literally the same, but the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a question of not literally the same. It simply isn't close enough the same to be fair to the -- I'm not suggesting it's done deliberately. It demonstrates the importance of keeping very closely. After all, this whole line of examination which does involve my not objecting to the Prosecution already straying over the conventional boundaries in relation to the examination of their own witnesses has involved a certain amount of textual analysis in the course of question and answer of the witness. And given that that is the whole basis of the questioning, it is essential to be careful about the summaries and paraphrases of the material in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it clear to everyone now what the difference is? I do understand that document was brought, but whether someone said something at that moment or that he brought it in order to, without perhaps saying so, that's the issue. Mr. Tieger. You will have understood the issue, and let's see how far we come. But you're looking at the clock, I wouldn't say desperately, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The question is, if we're going to break now, I'm actually going to take a closer look at the transcript and see if this issue needs further clarification. Otherwise I'm inclined to move on to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next subject. Then we'll adjourn until 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm not going to make any point out of it at this moment, the 21st of October submission ends for the reasons set out above the Prosecution informs the Trial Chamber of its intention to seek leave." That's different language from -- it's not -- it seems that a kind of practice has developed at this moment, and let's leave it at this. But that's what confused me a bit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, just to round out the issue we were discussing before the recess: Is it correct that whenever the ARK Crisis Staff wanted to implement anything, they would say that the order came from Pale? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether that was true or not is a different matter. I can't guarantee that that was actually how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also the case that Pale sometimes communicated directly with municipalities?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: On rare occasions. And I'm saying that from the aspects of Banja Luka, which is where I was. Rarely, because there were lines, deputy chains, executive government chains, party chains. But with the presidents of the municipalities on rare occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just quote directly what you stated on a previous occasion and ask you if that's accurate. Turning to page 22140 of the Brdjanin testimony. You were asked, beginning at page -- at line 1, extending down to about line 10 or so, you were asked about the chain of command. The question is: "Q. No. Again, I'm not suggesting that it was any different anywhere else but I just want to deal with what happened in the Serbian republic. It was transmitted down the chain of command. That chain of command included the regional, municipal, and local communities; is that right?" "A. Not really. It was not exactly a rule. The regional would sometimes be skipped and then we would receive it directly here at the municipal level." And just to complete your answer: "And then when they were not satisfied with the work of the individual municipalities, and the implementation of individual decisions, then -- I mean, I don't think that the chain was always respected, that it was the top and then us, that they suggested directly to us that something needed to be done." So is that essentially correct, Mr. Radic, that sometimes the regional level was skipped and instructions or orders would be received directly at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said in my previous answer, that it happened rarely, on occasion, from time to time, and not as a general rule. And so I said that in the conversation, in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And when the municipalities received an order or instruction directly from the republic level, that's what had to be done by the municipalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in some cases, or at least in one case, the municipality had a direct link to the republican level, to Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: When necessary, we did, and we used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the case of Prijedor, for example, their deputy, their assembly deputy, had a radio set to regularly report to Pale what was happening in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, not the deputies. If the municipality didn't have any links to Pale, then it did have radio links. It had to have some sort of connection and link. So yes, there was a case in which somebody did have a radio set link when it came to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was the deputy Mr. Srdic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That's what they said. I didn't see him speaking on the radio, but they said that he did have a radio station through which he was able to communicate with Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the context of learning about the radio that Mr. Srdic had was a warning by others to you that you should watch what you say around Mr. Srdic because he was reporting to Pale?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the stories going around, the rumours, that one should be wary of that particular gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mr. Radic, those weren't just general rumours; that was information you received from Mr. Srdic's fellow deputies; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Not only from them. It was going round Prijedor, and I took note of it, and possibly one of the deputies might have said it too. But I don't want to go into that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, you say possibly one of the deputies said it. But you said in a previous interview, the one conducted on July 16th, 2001, that you knew that because his colleagues, his fellow deputies, knew it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, if I said that, then that's how it was. So the deputies knew that the gentleman had this, and they conveyed that to me, and I knew about that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just for the Court's benefit, I'm referring to page 56 of the July 2001 interview, beginning at line 21. Ms. Korner asks: "Q. How do you know that the deputy for Prijedor had a radio set by which he communicated with Pale?"

utterances.speaker: MR. RADIC SAID
utterances.text: "A. His colleagues, his fellow deputies know." Question by Ms. Korner: "Q. How do you know?" "A. Because his fellow deputies told me that he is to be very -- I should be very careful around him and not talk about anything." And then Mr. Radic goes on to identify the deputy as Mr. Srdic. Mr. Radic, you indicated -- I think we cited a passage from an earlier interview regarding Mr. Brdjanin, and I think you indicated in your previous testimony that Mr. Brdjanin was a powerful man. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I never said he was powerful. He wasn't really powerful. His power was based on upon -- I've already told what it was based on, on the fact that he was a deputy. He was a minister. He was the vice-premier. So his power did not emanate from the fact that he was president of the Crisis Staff and I never considered him to be a powerful man, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I was referring to page 22127 of the -- of your testimony during Brdjanin, at lines 4 through 11, where you were asked: "Q. Yes, I am. And so what you were saying there was that the authority of Mr. Brdjanin and others in the regional Crisis Staff came from their positions as deputies and ministers; is that right?" Your answer was: "A. Yes, the authority of Mr. Brdjanin. The previous question was that it was true to say that Mr. Brdjanin was a very powerful man. I said that his authority wasn't as a result of his being president of the Crisis Staff; it was a result of him having role of minister, et cetera, and that is where he derived his authority from."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything different from that a moment ago, that the source of his power was -- did not lie in the Crisis Staff, but rather in the functions that he had and performed. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, part of your answer was: "I never said he was powerful." In the part just read to you, you say: "It was true to say that Mr. Brdjanin was a very powerful man." That is not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: And, in continuation, Your Honour, I said his power emanated from the functions he held. So that was the sense of his power and where his power lay and was derived from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But saying: I never said he was a powerful man, and saying: It's true to say that he was powerful. That's totally different. If there are good explanations on where his power came from, whatever, but that is really contradicting each other. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on a number of occasions during the course of interview with representatives of the Prosecutor in July 2001, you pointed the same thing out, that the authority in power of Mr. Brdjanin and others was derived from their positions as deputies or ministers. And we point you, for example, to page 60 of the July 2001 transcript, lines 11 through 15, where you say: "A. No. What I claim is one other thing. What I claim is that the authority of the accused, that their authority was not -- they didn't derive their authority from this, this two- or three-month-old institution, quasi-institution of Crisis Staff. Their authorities derive from higher positions, assembly, deputy, ministerial. All of this was just --" And Ms. Korner says: "Q. All right." And that's the point you were trying to make during the course of that interview and also during the course of your testimony; is that correct? I see you nodding, but I just need an oral --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct, Mr. Radic, that the link between the leadership of the country and the people on the ground were the deputies?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it was logical that if you go to the Assembly, then if they go to the Assembly, then they convey what the Assembly had decided upon, and that they insisted that this should be implemented further down the line, what the Assembly of Republika Srpska had decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I appreciate that, but the question goes beyond the logic of the situation and what can be concluded logically from that information. But it also goes into what you saw and observed and learned from your own position. And in that respect, let me direct your attention to page 4 of the July 2001 interview, when you were asked about the order on establishing crisis staffs. And the question beginning at line 32 of page 4 was: "And how did that order, how was that order received?" And your answer was: "I couldn't tell you that, because the link between the leadership of the country and the people on the ground were deputies." And you go on to say: "A document just arrived to say that they wanted to know the structure and who exactly was in the Crisis Staff." In addition to the logic that might be applied to this situation, is it correct to say that it was your observation during 1992 that the link between the leadership of the country and the people on the ground were the deputies?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question was asked about -- it's at 18:11:29. The exact question has been asked and he answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And he's now being confronted with a statement he gave and the question is asked again to him. You may proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall the -- if you recall the question, you can just answer.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it's logical, as I say. Once they come back from the national assembly, it would be logical for them to tell us what was decided upon up above. So in a sense, they were a link between the national assembly on the one hand, and the top leadership on the other, with us down below. I said that last time and I repeat it today. So the deputies were, in actual fact, the people who conveyed to us what was going on and what decisions and conclusions had been made. And amongst others, we have this decision on the formation of the staffs, et cetera, et cetera, where they too had a certain number of seats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just try to find out whether I understood you well. Is your testimony that you said this is what was logic and that's what I saw to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated earlier that whenever members of the ARK Crisis Staff wanted to implement something, they would say it arrived from Pale and it had to be implemented. Is it correct that it would be an Assembly deputy or a minister who would come and say: This is what they've ordered from above, and this is how it will be implemented?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was necessarily a deputy. It could have been anyone else from the political leadership, not just from the ranks of the deputies. Naturally, when they returned, they could, of course, convey to us the decisions as to what needed to be done in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it would have been one of those with contacts with Pale, a deputy, a minister, or someone else in the leadership, who would come and say: This is what they've ordered from above, and this is how it has to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that they would necessarily verbally convey it to us. There would be a document that would be brought to the Crisis Staff, although it is possible that sometimes they used -- by virtue of their position, they conveyed to us a piece of information that did not necessarily have to originate from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention - maybe this will help - to another portion of the interview of July 2001. That's on page 44. And I'll begin at line 14. Question by Ms. Korner: "So did you see the order from Pale before the meeting or after the meeting?" Your answer: "Whenever they wanted to implement something, they would say that it had arrived from Pale and that had it to be implemented, always." Then question: "Yes, but who would say that? Was it Brdjanin? Was it Kupresanin?" Your answer: "I couldn't tell you for sure, but it would have been one of those who had contacts with Pale, an Assembly deputy or minister, and they would always come and say: This is what the -- they've ordered from above, and this is how it will be implemented." That's right, isn't it? That's what you said, and that's correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the deputies actually considered themselves more important than the people at the municipal level; isn't that right? And that's how they thought of themselves and that's how they behaved.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, they were deputies to the People's Assembly, and therefore, in terms of hierarchy, they were superior to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, they were not only superior; they were virtually untouchable, weren't they? Isn't that something you said before, and didn't you call them "the Russian Deputates"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes they did behave this way. They would go to a meeting, come back, and convey to us something that had been said up above. Whether it actually had been said or not, we did not know. But that was the way they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Radic, when you were asked during your July interview who had the power to direct events in Banja Luka and the surrounding area, you said: "The police, the military, and the deputies had a large influence." Isn't that right? And let me direct your attention to that specific site. Page 32, beginning at line 21. Ms. Korner: "Right. Who do you say did have the power to direct what happened in the area of the ARK in the various -- well, first of all let us take it separately. I'm sorry. Banja Luka." Your answer: "The police did, the military did. Deputies had very large influence. Here in the municipality, we have the authority to take care of the local economy, of everything that was in the municipal Statute which had not been changed since before the war." That's correct, is it not, that the deputies had a very large impact and influence over what happened in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Let us take the order that I used, the police and the military. You need not emphasise why they had influence at a time of war. But equally so, the deputies brought over information decided upon at the Assembly, and that's why they had the power. Even before the war, during the war, and now after the war, they have power locally, just as they did before the war, before the 1990s. They had the authority to deal with the local issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So at least part of their power derived from the fact that they were receiving the instructions of the leadership and conveying it to the ground.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: They would come to us with the freshest of information from the meetings of the -- from the sessions of the Assembly, from government meetings where decision were taken, telling us whatever took place at the level of the government. Because the presidents of the municipalities had nothing to do with the Assembly level unless they had some specific matters that they had to deal with directly with that level of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So they would -- is it correct that they would bring this information, they would say it had to be implemented, and they acted in a fashion that indicated that they expected it to be implemented?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: They could expect so, and in some places these decisions were indeed implemented. But in those places where people in the leadership had their own minds, they wouldn't implement them. Of course, the Assembly level was of decisive importance. It is also true that sometimes they did behave in such a stuck-up way; that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And part of the reason that the deputies had such power locally and acted in such a fashion is because, in your words, they had a masterful leader in Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: He was their president, the president of the National Assembly. It doesn't go to say that whatever decisions were taken locally originated from the leaders. Of course, the president of the National Assembly was their superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Radic, I'm going to direct your attention to another exchange in the July 2001 interview, one that I'd suggest to you suggests that your view about that issue was -- had something more -- was dealt with something more than his position as president only. And let me direct your attention to page 62, beginning at line 26: "Of course we were at a lower level for them, the municipal level, and that's how they acted. You'll see -- I don't know who of the deputies you summoned, but you'll see even today they think they are something better than others because they were elected the one time in 1990, and they continued to rule until 1996. And if they have a masterful leader like Krajisnik, then -- Question: "Who was a masterful leader?" And your answer is: "The deputies. Question: "Like Krajisnik? You say: "He was their president. Again, I repeat: You're just wasting your time with the crisis staffs. Everything was planned up from above." Mr. Radic, weren't you indicating in that answer that the focus should be on the instructions that were being given from above, including Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you: We are levelling up now the leaders and the presidents of the Assembly. It is true that he was a president of the Assembly, but I've never said that whatever decisions were taken locally originated from him. Because he had the rules of procedure, he had the statute, and he had to act within the legal remit. I have a document Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that was adopted by the National Assembly and signed by Krajisnik which goes beyond the remit of the statute and the rules of procedure. So I never said that he was the leader, the mastermind behind their acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting to hear you say that, Mr. Radic, because didn't you also say that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That's common knowledge. That's no secret. It was Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic, and Mr. Karadzic. They were the Presidency. There are no new matters to be discovered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And it was the Presidency that could exert influence over the police and the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Now, what it was that the Presidency could do, it is difficult for me to answer that one, because I am not familiar with the work of the Presidency. Most probably, they had to have influence over the military as the supreme body. Now, who from among the members of the Presidency had the role of coordinating the army is something I cannot tell you. That is something you need to consult the rules of procedure of the Presidency, where it states the roles of different members. The same is true for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, let me move on to a slightly different topic and ask to have marked next in order B09-8148 through 8153.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the reference is in an answer given a few moments ago. It's line 15. It's 18:27:33. It's page 69, line 15. The transcript says: "I have a document that was adopted by the National Assembly and signed by Krajisnik." And Ms. Cmeric informs me that the original Serbian actually had the sense of: I would like to see a document. Which is clearly very different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was your testimony that you would like to see any document in which Mr. Krajisnik would go beyond what was in accordance with the procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. That's what I wanted to say, what I actually said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, of course I noticed that logic is not the answer to everything, but that answer has some logic in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, I know you had an opportunity to see this document during the course of your testimony in the Brdjanin case. Do you need any further time to review it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Registrar informs me that this document was already Exhibit Number P209, so we leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just direct your attention to one part of that document quickly, Mr. Radic, and that is the list of non-Serbs from Prijedor. 42.000 Muslims and 2.000 Croats are listed as, in the language of the document, "moved out from Prijedor." In fact, this document indicates 44.000 non-Serbs who had been expelled from Prijedor by 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That's what it says. This was compiled by the Ministry of the Interior, Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's consistent with your own understanding and observations of what happened in Prijedor in 1992 and 1993; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the same is true for the remainder of the document as well. That's consistent with your observations at the time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Which observations are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, for one thing, you saw some of those people deported, didn't you, deported in cattle cars?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the expulsion of these non-Serbs from Prijedor and Kljuc and Sanski Most listed in the document, there were also large-scale murders of non-Serbs during operations conducted by Serb police and army forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in addition, civilian non-Serbs were put in camps; and you yourself had an opportunity to visit one such camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was a visit to Omarska in July of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Omarska was run by the police and the military; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Mostly by the police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you received permission from -- or you sought and received permission from the military to visit Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there you saw civilians confined in conditions that were clearly inappropriate for human beings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, even before your visit, you had some information about the number of people held there and the conditions, because quite a number of Muslims from Prijedor had informed you of that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Indeed, even Serbs who lived in Omarska asked -- or some Serbs who lived in Omarska asked the authorities in Banja Luka to transfer Muslims from Omarska camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: They could not ask anything from the Banja Luka authorities because it did not lie within their authority. It lay within the authority of Prijedor, and it could have been done both by the police and the military, and the Banja Luka authorities did their best under the circumstances. Because the Banja Luka authorities had no authority whatsoever in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. The point of my question, in part, was that at least some Serbs came to the Banja Luka authorities to report what was happening in Omarska and seek some kind of assistance for the Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you again: They did not seek that from the Banja Luka authorities but from the authorities that were in Banja Luka, to see what they could do about it. It doesn't mean that these were the -- that this was the Assembly of Banja Luka. But there were Muslims who had relatives in Prijedor who came to see us to inquire of their relatives there, and these were the people that I knew both in Prijedor and in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, when you visited Omarska, in addition to seeing the conditions that prevailed there, was it also the case that prisoners were abused before your very eyes by being forced to sing Serbian national songs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That they did, but they were not harassed physically. I held it against them because I thought it amounted to psychological abuse for the people to sing the kind of songs they are not in favour of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You recognise that for what it was, an effort to humiliate these prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: There is nothing for me to recognise there. I've told you that I myself thought that it amounted to psychological and mental abuse and I thought that an end must be put to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, among the others in your delegation was Mr. Zupljanin, correct, the head of the CSB?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Correct, because the police was involved in interrogations there, and we went over there to see how it went along.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you express your disapproval to Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I expressed my disapproval to all of them, particularly to the Prijedor leadership, and I told them that they must look for an adequate solution for these people as soon as possible. Upon my return to Banja Luka, I came to the head of the Red Cross office to tell them that they should do everything in their power to alleviate the situation of the people. It was Mr. Minik [phoen]. He was the chief of the Red Cross in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't specifically ask Mr. Zupljanin to do something about it because he had his own hierarchy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I could only apply to the police, just as one could before the war, during the war, and after the war. You could only apply to the police to do something, ask them to do something, but they were never under the local authority. Because the you have the republican Ministry of the Interior and then the lines down to the field. The local authorities have nothing to do with the police. You could deduce that from the statutes as of before the war, during the war, and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And everything that was done in Krajina by the police had to be verified in Pale by the Minister of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, because he was the one who in fact coordinated everything. I suppose so, because there was nobody else in the government who was in charge of the police and the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At any rate, that was your understanding in 1992 of how the hierarchy worked; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I was aware of it immediately because the only town that did not have the public security service was Banja Luka, because it was there that the security services centre was in place for the 20 municipalities. So that you had nobody to appeal to to bring law and order to the major town in Republika Srpska. But that's the way things happened, and that's the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So focusing now on the hierarchy of the Ministry of the Interior, essentially, instructions would come down from the Minister of the Interior to the CSB, and then from there to the local level, and reports went back up?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have marked as Prosecution's next in order an article from Kozarski Vjesnik dated July 17th, 1992, and bearing ERN of 0300-3570.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be number --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, P361 is an article from Kozarski Vjesnik which reflects the visit to Omarska by you and others, about which we've just spoken; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I'm just reading it. May I be allowed to read through it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I assume that you're referring to this article here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm referring to a article headlined "Krajina representatives in Prijedor."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the article indicates that you, Mr. Zupljanin, Dr. Vukic, and Mr. Brdjanin were the members -- were the representatives from the Autonomous Region of Krajina who visited Prijedor on the day we've spoken of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how quickly the witness is reading, but he wasn't given very long to read an article that he said he wanted to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I responded to something the witness had said, but I'm more than happy to give him as much time to review it as may be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, whenever you feel you need more time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger grants you then you may address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that was an accurate reflection of who the members of the visiting party were.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to direct your attention to some remarks by Mr. Brdjanin as he's quoted in the article. And to orient you, there seems to be a sub-headline called "Nobody finds it easy." And then I would direct your attention to a portion of the article which is the fourth paragraph below that and begins with Mr. Brdjanin's name.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: So it's not this article here, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's a good question. So let's make sure we're talking about precisely the same thing. And I may be in fact directing your attention to what has been put together as one article, but in fact reflected as more than one there. So, as you know, I first directed your attention to --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've found it. Here it is. I had to read through it to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you find the particular paragraph that begins with Mr. Brdjanin's name, full name, Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that you're drawing my attention to this portion here, and the assertion made by Mr. Brdjanin. And the quotation: "What we have seen in Prijedor is an example of a job well done and it is a pity that many in Banja Luka are not aware of it yet," et cetera, et cetera, and then "there is constantly growing number of superfluous Muslims in Banja Luka," et cetera, et cetera. Did you have that in mind? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's precisely the portion I wanted to direct your attention to.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: And that follows the style of Mr. Brdjanin generally. I have nothing more to say on that. The only thing correct here is that what was happening around Banja Luka meant that we were subject to a large number of refugees coming into Banja Luka looking for safety and salvation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I pause for just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I'm moving on to another portion, which I think would be difficult to compress in five minutes and is probably significant enough to ensure that we do it in one portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do so, Mr. Tieger, I find a -- oh, yes. It's the whole of the newspaper that in four pages and only the front page, I take it, translated. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can double-check, but that is my understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's the left side of the first page which is translated. But perhaps you could ask -- the witness doesn't know what is translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, what I certainly can do is simply get that checked before tomorrow morning and answer the Court's inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Radic, it's close to 7.00. We'll finish for the day. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony, the testimony you have already given today and you're still about to give tomorrow. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Radic out of the courtroom. Mr. Radic, you're expected to be here tomorrow at 9.00 in Courtroom I. So we start tomorrow in the morning and not in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, Mr. Radic has been scheduled for four hours. Could you give us an indication on how much time you would still need tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be optimistic, I don't know how much time I've used, but as the Court knows I've been pretty rigorous about coming in under the time. I think we will with him finish in the first session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could well bring us over four hours, but -- today we had a late start. We started at 2.30. We then spent some ten to fifteen minutes on procedural issues and then the remaining time, because of the late start of the last portion of today, we lost altogether approximately 40 minutes of the four hours' court time we usually have, apart from the last three minutes. So that would bring us to three hours and twenty minutes now. If you had you would add the whole of the first session tomorrow morning, that would bring another one hour and a half, which would bring us to 4 hours and 5 minutes. But Madam Registrar is always more precise in her ... Well, she is more generous to you. Three hours and ten minutes in chief until now; one and a half extra, that would bring us well over four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- first of all, it's always a mistake to compliment yourself in advance and I've certainly learned my lesson in that respect. I'm trying to make the examination as efficient as possible. I think I'm trying to indicate to the Court that it's going to be in the reasonable range of that four-hour estimate. Even though - and I would remind the Court - I think we tried to indicate it's quite difficult under such circumstances to make an estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. What I was seeking was to encourage you to say what you've just said. If there are no further issues, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of October, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
